reading.name: United States
reading.headline: United States is in the Elevated tier (43/100, 92nd riskiest of 203; 1st of 2 in North America). Material risk on more than one front.
reading.ground: Expect periodic protests, policy surprises or economic stress. Contracts and plans can be upset by events outside your control, so they need contingencies and regular review.

drivers.label: Macroeconomic & Financial
drivers.ground: Exposure to an economic crisis: prices rising fast, a falling currency, shortages of dollars, tax rises or spending cuts, and payments that arrive late or not at all.
drivers.felt_by: Anyone who earns, saves, borrows or trades in the local currency, importers most of all.
evidence: a large budget deficit (-8.5% of GDP)

warnings.label: Thin FX reserves (<3 months of imports)
warnings.meaning: The central bank has little foreign currency left: less than three months of imports. Import restrictions, dollar shortages, capital controls or a devaluation often follow.
warnings.response: Firms keep extra stock of imported inputs, convert local earnings to hard currency promptly, and check the rules on moving money out of the country.

warnings.label: High public debt (≥90% of GDP)
warnings.meaning: Public debt is high, leaving little room to respond to a shock. Tax rises, spending cuts or an IMF programme become more likely, and in the worst case a debt restructuring.
warnings.response: Investors check their exposure to government bonds and public-sector clients, and treat budget announcements and IMF talks as risk events.

warnings.label: Large fiscal deficit (≥5% of GDP)
warnings.meaning: The government spends far more than it collects. That usually ends in tax rises, spending cuts, money printing or late payments to suppliers.
warnings.response: Suppliers tighten payment terms with government clients and plan for tax changes.

direction: Over the longer run it has risen from 33 in 2015 to 43 now.

business: Use the score to decide where to look closer: compare with peers (Peers tab) and read the drivers before deciding anything.
Protect against currency and payment risk: price in hard currency or index to inflation, shorten payment terms, consider hedging, and check the rules on moving money out.
Thin reserves often come before import limits or a devaluation: hold extra stock of imported inputs and convert local earnings promptly.
Expect tax rises, spending cuts or late government payments: check your exposure to public-sector clients and contracts.
ngo: A development setting: focus on long-term programmes and local partners.
travel: Check your government's official travel advice for United States before you go. It changes far faster than annual data.
Bring more than one way to pay: cash shortages, card problems and fast-changing prices are possible.
research: Start with the drivers: Macroeconomic & Financial carries the most risk. Explain why.
Put it in context: United States ranks 1st of 2 in North America and the Peers tab shows who is close.
Check whether changes are real: governance moves inside the WGI confidence intervals may be noise (Data tab, Governance).
Test the drivers: the What-if simulator shows which indicators would move the score most.
Write it up: the Assessment builder turns this into a structured brief with probabilities.

caveats: Scores are relative: they show where a country sits among the others and give no probability of any event.
The data look backwards: governance scores describe last year and conflict data lag by up to two years. Check current news and official travel advice.
This is general, educational guidance. It is not investment, legal or security advice.
